title: Lines and Angles — Chapter Summary
intro: Geometry begins with the simplest objects: a point, a line, a line segment and a ray. From them we build angles — the spaces between two rays meeting at a common endpoint. This chapter teaches you to NAME, MEASURE and CLASSIFY angles, and introduces the special pairs of angles formed when two lines meet.

sections.heading: Point, Line, Segment, Ray
bullets: Point: a position with no length or width.
Line: extends without end in both directions; no endpoints.
Line segment: piece of a line with two endpoints; has finite length.
Ray: piece of a line with one endpoint; extends without end in the other direction.
Compare: point (0 endpoints, 0 length); line (0 endpoints, infinite); ray (1 endpoint, infinite); segment (2 endpoints, finite).

sections.heading: Angles — Definition and Naming
bullets: An angle is formed by two rays sharing the same endpoint.
The shared endpoint is the VERTEX; the rays are the ARMS.
Naming: ∠ABC means the angle whose vertex is B (the middle letter).
If only one angle has vertex B, we may write ∠B.
Arm length does NOT affect the size of the angle — only the OPENING does.

sections.heading: Measuring with a Protractor
bullets: Angles are measured in DEGREES (°).
Full turn = 360°; half turn = 180°; quarter turn = 90°.
A protractor is a half-circle tool from 0° to 180°.
Steps to measure: (1) place protractor centre on vertex; (2) align 0° with one arm; (3) read where the other arm crosses; (4) use the correct (inner/outer) scale.
Drawing: same idea — mark a dot at the desired degree, then draw a ray from the vertex through it.

sections.heading: Types of Angles
bullets: Zero: 0°.
Acute: greater than 0° and less than 90°. Examples: 30°, 45°, 60°.
Right: exactly 90°. Marked with a small square.
Obtuse: greater than 90° and less than 180°. Examples: 100°, 135°.
Straight: exactly 180°.
Reflex: greater than 180° and less than 360°.
Complete: exactly 360° (full turn).
Memory aid: acute = sharp; obtuse = blunt; reflex = more than half a turn.

sections.heading: Parallel, Intersecting, Perpendicular Lines
bullets: Parallel: two lines that never meet (e.g. railway tracks). Symbol: ∥.
Intersecting: two lines that cross at exactly one point.
Perpendicular: intersecting lines that meet at a RIGHT angle (90°). Symbol: ⊥.
Perpendicular is a special case of intersecting.
In a flat plane, two non-intersecting lines must be parallel.

sections.heading: Angles at an Intersection
bullets: When two straight lines cross, they make FOUR angles around the crossing point.
Linear pair: two adjacent angles forming a straight line — they sum to 180°.
Vertically opposite: angles directly across — they are EQUAL.
From ONE angle you can find all four: opposite is equal, neighbours are 180°-minus-it.
Example: if one angle is 70°, the four angles are 70°, 110°, 70°, 110°.

key_takeaways: Point / line / segment / ray have 0, 0, 2, 1 endpoints respectively.
An angle has a vertex (middle letter when naming) and two arms.
Angles measured in degrees; full turn = 360°.
Acute < 90°; right = 90°; obtuse between 90° and 180°; straight = 180°; reflex between 180° and 360°.
Parallel lines never meet; perpendicular = intersecting at 90°.
At an intersection: linear pair sums to 180°; vertically opposite angles are equal.

glossary.definition: A position with no length or width.
A straight path that extends without end in both directions; no endpoints.
Part of a line with two endpoints and a definite length.
Part of a line with one endpoint, extending without end in the other direction.
The figure formed by two rays sharing a common endpoint.
The shared endpoint of the two rays of an angle.
Either of the two rays that form the angle.
The unit of angle measure; one full turn = 360°.
A half-circle measuring tool with degree marks from 0° to 180°.
Two lines in the same plane that never meet, no matter how far they are extended (∥).
Two lines that intersect at a right angle (⊥, 90°).
Two lines that cross at exactly one point (the point of intersection).
Two adjacent angles whose non-common arms form a straight line; they sum to 180°.
Angles directly across from each other when two lines intersect; they are equal.
